title: Res judicata - why the same dispute can't be litigated twice
p1:
Can a person keep taking the same case to court again and again until they get a different result?

Surprisingly, the law says no. A dispute that has already been finally decided cannot simply be reopened under a new strategy.
p2: Many people think losing a case means they can just file another one with slightly different arguments. But the principle of res judicata prevents this. It means that once a competent court has finally decided an issue between the same parties, that same matter cannot be litigated again.
p3:
The reason behind this rule is simple: courts need finality. Without it, lawsuits could continue forever, wasting time and resources for everyone involved. The interesting part is that res judicata can apply even when a party tries to present old issues in a new form.

The takeaway: winning a case is not just about the judgment itself; it can also close the door on future attempts to fight the same battle again.
conclusion: Do you think this rule protects people from endless litigation, or could it sometimes prevent someone from getting another chance in court?
